reason: The airways end beside the sacs, so joining them should establish the air route.
expectation: The airways will connect to the lung air sacs.

effect: The airways and sacs form an air route with an empty exchange-surface slot. The result also explains why many small sacs provide more surface area.
reaction: The equal-volume comparison is a useful way to make the surface-area advantage clear.
reason: The thin exchange lining appears to form the air-facing part of the missing exchange surface.
expectation: The lining will be fitted to the air sacs as part of the exchange surface.

effect: The air route now has its thin lining, but the capillary mesh is still missing.
reaction: The result makes the next part of the exchange surface clear.
reason: The capillary mesh surrounds the sacs and supplies the blood-facing side of the exchange surface.
expectation: The mesh will attach around the lined air sacs to form an exchange surface.

effect: The lung route now has an exchange surface where air and blood occupy separate spaces; it still needs a connection to the circulating blood.
reaction: The separate spaces make the chapter’s title clearer.
reason: The lung capillaries need to connect to the vessel circuit so blood can reach the exchange surface.
expectation: The lung capillary mesh will connect to the blood circuit.

effect: The vessel circuit has no available combination yet, so I need to continue building the lung setup first.
reaction: I was surprised that the blood circuit cannot connect at this stage.
reason: The pleural membranes link the lung side to the chest side, so they seem like the next part needed to renew the air.
expectation: The membranes will attach around the lung route, preparing it to connect to the breathing chest.

effect: The pleural membranes now surround the lung, with their outer sheet ready to couple to the chest.
reaction: The description makes the next connection clear.
reason: The breathing chest can couple to the pleura to renew the air in the lung route.
expectation: The chest will connect to the lung through the pleural membranes, allowing its movement to renew the air.

effect: The chest now moves the lungs through the pleural surfaces, renewing air, and the new goal is to carry oxygen to the working body.
reaction: The pressure gauge helps explain how chest movement draws air in.
reason: The breathing lungs now appear ready to connect to the blood circuit for oxygen transport.
expectation: The lung capillaries will connect to the circulating blood so it can carry oxygen to the body.

effect: Connecting the breathing lungs to the vessel circuit completed the oxygen-delivery route and both chapter goals. The final picture traces oxygen from the lungs to tissues and blood back to the heart.
reaction: Seeing the lung and body circuits joined was satisfying, although the earlier unavailable connection left me unsure why the chest had to be added first.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting the breathing chest to the lungs was most worthwhile: the pressure gauge and pleural movement explained how chest expansion draws air in.

leastWorthwhile.text: Adding the lining and capillary mesh felt a little repetitive, though each contributed a distinct part of the exchange surface.

surprise.text: I was surprised that the vessel circuit could not connect to the lung route before the breathing chest was added.

arbitrary.text: The required order for connecting circulation felt somewhat arbitrary: the result at step 4 did not explain why the connection was unavailable.

continue.text: I would probably continue for another chapter. The final circulation route connected several earlier constructions, and I would be curious to see how the body uses the delivered supplies.
